doc.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Artie Shaw's band and Roy Eldridge sitting in in Phoenix
summary: Playing the swing shift after Artie Shaw at the main dance hall, and Roy Eldridge coming to the little club and playing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Were you playing for predominately black or did you play for white audiences too?

Yes. Some, some. I remember the main dance hall there where all the big bands came to play on the one-nighters, we played there. One night, a very nice band lead by Artie Shaw came and played, and they played from 9-1, and then we played what’s called the “swing shift” from 1-5. So, we were up there playing, and all these guys from Artie Shaw’s band were standing around listening to us, and we thought, well we must be really good [laughs]. Roy Eldridge was a member of the band, and he came to the little joint where I was playing. He’d sit around a while, had a couple beers, and then he got up and played the drums. He was enjoying himself so much, he went to his room, he was staying in the doctor’s house ‘cause there was no black hotels, he went and got his horn and came back and played. Now, here’s one of the greatest trumpet players in the world coming in and playing with me. I was 99% sure ignorance, but that’s the way people were. It was great.
Did you talk to him about playing trumpet?
Yes, I talked to him. I asked him whatever I could ask, not so much ‘cause you have to know something to even ask the right questions.
Do you remember anything he told you during that first encounter?
No, no, I just remember the first question I asked was, “How long have you been playing the trumpet?” He said, “As long as baseball” [laughs]. But he was not a very nice guy.
[Laughs] Okay. So, that must’ve been the first time you heard a professional jazz band live, is that correct?
